overview.section: 8.2 Training a convnet from scratch on a small dataset
overview.main_topic: Step-by-step Kaggle download in Colab (join the competition, API key, login, download, unzip) and a first look at the raw images
overview.central_idea: After accepting the competition rules and creating an API key, three short snippets log in with kagglehub, download the competition files, and extract train.zip. The resulting images are medium-resolution color JPEGs of varying sizes, colours and backgrounds.

learning_objectives: Carry out the two prerequisites for Kaggle competition downloads (join the competition, generate an API key)
Extract a zip archive with Python's zipfile module

summary:
This page completes the sidebar **"Downloading a Kaggle dataset in Google Colaboratory"** begun on p.266. Two preparation steps come first:

1. Go to `https://www.kaggle.com/c/dogs-vs-cats/rules` and click **Join the Competition**. Competition data can only be downloaded after accepting the rules.
2. Go to `https://www.kaggle.com/settings` and **generate a Kaggle API key**.

Then, in the notebook:

- `import kagglehub` and `kagglehub.login()` authenticate with the API key.
- `download_path = kagglehub.competition_download("dogs-vs-cats")` downloads the competition files. They are two archives, **`train.zip`** (training data) and **`test1.zip`** (test data). Only the training data is used.
- The `zipfile` module opens `download_path + "/train.zip"` and calls `extractall(".")`, which unpacks the images into the current directory.

"All done!" closes the sidebar.

Back in the main text, the authors note that the pictures are **medium-resolution color JPEGs**. **Figure 8.8** shows several samples: cats in a basket and on a bed, dogs outdoors and being held. The caption stresses that sizes were not modified and that the samples **come in different sizes, colors, backgrounds, etc.** This heterogeneity is what a real image dataset looks like. It is also why the images will later have to be resized to a common shape (180 × 180, p.269) and batched before they can go into a ConvNet. The labelled train archive is used because test1.zip comes from the competition's held-out set (which has no labels); the authors build their own train/validation/test subsets from train.zip on p.268.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The pictures are medium-resolution color JPEGs. Figure 8.8 shows examples whose sizes weren't modified; they come in different sizes, colors, backgrounds, etc.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Unlike MNIST's uniform 28 × 28 grayscale digits, these are three-channel photographs with arbitrary width and height, varied poses and cluttered backgrounds. A model must be invariant to all of this to tell cats from dogs.

concepts.name: Programmatic dataset download (kagglehub)
concepts.definition: Using Kaggle's Python package to authenticate and download competition data from code.

import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile(download_path + "/train.zip", "r") as zip_ref:

deeper.title: From download to model-ready data
deeper.body:
1. Join the competition, create an API key (this page).
2. Log in, download, unzip train.zip (this page).
3. Subsample 1,000/500/1,000 images per class into train/validation/test folders (p.268).
4. Load the folders as batched, resized tensors (p.271).
5. Train the ConvNet (p.269 onward).

questions.question: What two things must you do on the Kaggle website before downloading the data from code?
questions.answer: Join the competition (accept the rules) at kaggle.com/c/dogs-vs-cats/rules, and generate an API key at kaggle.com/settings.
questions.explanation: These are steps 1 and 2 at the top of the page.

questions.question: Which files does kagglehub.competition_download("dogs-vs-cats") produce?
questions.explanation: The page says it downloads train.zip and test1.zip. The split folders are created later by the authors (p.268), and no npz or TFRecord file is involved.

questions.question: Why does the chapter only use train.zip?
questions.answer: It contains the labelled images. The authors build their own training, validation and test subsets from it (p.268). The competition test images are not needed.
questions.explanation: The book says 'We'll only use the training data here'. The note that the competition test set is unlabeled is an explanation beyond the book.

questions.question: What does figure 8.8 tell you about the preprocessing that will be required?
questions.answer: The images differ in size, colour and background, so they must be decoded and resized to a common shape (180 × 180 on p.269) before they can be batched as tensors.
questions.explanation: Neural networks need fixed-shape inputs within a batch.

questions.question: What does `zip_ref.extractall(".")` do?
options: Extracts all files from the archive into the current directory
Extracts only image files into a new temp directory
Deletes the zip after reading it
Loads the images into memory as a NumPy array
questions.answer: Extracts all files from the archive into the current directory
questions.explanation: '.' is the current working directory, and extractall extracts every member. It doesn't filter files, delete the archive or load arrays.

questions.question: Have you run these three snippets and checked that a train/ folder with about 25,000 JPEGs exists?
questions.answer: You should see files like cat.0.jpg … dog.12499.jpg (the file naming is used on p.268).
questions.explanation: The next listing depends on this directory being present.
